subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: After a year of Saturday coding classes in a community hall in Durban, Nour opened the attendance sheets with Lindiwe, a teacher at the local school. Forty-one children had come regularly. Six were girls. 'Why so few?' Nour asked. Lindiwe suggested asking the mothers, so they spent two weekends talking to families at the market and the bus rank. Several mothers said they wanted to know who ran the class before letting a daughter go, and Saturday afternoons were when girls were needed at home. Nour moved the class to Saturday morning, invited mothers to sit in on the first session, and asked a woman teacher, Thandi, to co-lead. Three months later the attendance sheet showed seventeen girls.

qa.q: How many of the regular children were girls after the first year?
qa.a: Six of the forty-one regular children were girls.

qa.q: What was Nour feeling when looking at the sheet?
qa.a: Nour was puzzled and concerned, shown by asking, 'Why so few?'

qa.q: What other approach could Nour use to learn more about why girls stayed away?
qa.a: Nour could also have a short chat with girls themselves, since their reasons may differ from what their mothers say.

qa.q: How might the mothers have seen the invitation to sit in?
qa.a: Several mothers were probably reassured, since they wanted to know who ran the class before letting a daughter go.

grounding: Shows a person using a year of attendance data to see that weekend classes reach few girls, and adding a timing and a woman teacher after hearing from mothers.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
"Four girls out of thirty-one," Pema read from the attendance register. The community hall in Gangtok was empty except for the plastic chairs and the two of them.
Jasleen leaned over. "A whole year, and only four?"
"I kept thinking girls weren't interested." Pema flipped through the pages. "But look, the four who come are all sisters of boys who come."
"So it's permission, not interest."
Pema nodded slowly. "Mothers told me the ten o'clock slot clashes with housework, and some didn't like that all our teachers are men."
"What if we added a two o'clock batch?" Jasleen said. "And I teach it."
Pema picked up a pen and crossed out the old timetable on the notice. "Two o'clock, Sundays, with Jasleen Ma'am. I'll visit ten homes this week and tell the mothers myself."

qa.q: How many girls were in the register out of thirty-one?
How did Pema feel on realising the four girls were all sisters of boys who come?
qa.a: Pema felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since the earlier guess that girls weren't interested turned out to be wrong.

qa.q: What else could Pema check after a few months, and why?
qa.a: Pema could count girls in the new batch each month, so the change is judged by evidence and not by hope.

qa.q: How might the mothers see the new two o'clock batch with Jasleen Ma'am?
qa.a: They may feel their worries were heard, and it becomes easier to say yes when the timing suits the household and a woman is teaching.

grounding: It shows an organiser noticing from a year of data that few girls attend, then adding a timing mothers can approve and a woman teacher.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
Dear Wasim,
You asked for an update on the Sunday science club before renewing your support, so here is the honest version.
After a year, we had 48 students on the register and only 6 girls. I had assumed that meant girls liked science less. Then I went door to door in Chas with Meenu, our only woman volunteer, and the mothers said the same two things: the club ended after dark, and there was no woman teacher.
So in March we moved the girls' batch to 3 p.m., ending before sunset, and Meenu now teaches it. I also started a simple sheet: names, attendance, and one line from each parent.
In three months, girls went from 6 to 19. That is not success yet, but it is the first number that has moved.
Thank you for waiting while I learned this.
Tanuja

qa.q: How many girls were on the register after the first year?
What did Tanuja feel after hearing the mothers door to door?
qa.a: Tanuja seems humbled and a little embarrassed, having assumed girls liked science less, and grateful to Wasim for waiting.

qa.q: What would you change first if girls' numbers stopped rising after the move?
qa.a: I would ask the new girls and their parents what still makes it hard, since the door-to-door talks were what revealed the real problem the first time.

qa.q: How might Wasim see this email before deciding to renew support?
qa.a: Wasim may trust the club more, because the email admits a wrong guess and shows a change based on evidence, with numbers to check.

grounding: It shows an organiser changing a club's timing and adding a woman teacher after a year of data showed few girls were attending.
